stances.claim: DOJ Secretary Remulla's Opinion No. 21 S2022 correctly opens RE (solar, wind, hydro, ocean/tidal) to foreign EDU. His statutory-construction reasoning -- that 'natural resources' under Article XII §2 must be read via noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis to mean only resources sharing the characteristic of being 'susceptible to appropriation' (like lands, fisheries, forests, wildlife) -- places sun, wind, and ocean outside the enumeration because 'they are not subject to appropriation.'

Remulla further argues that the constitutional phrase 'all forces of potential energy' refers only to position-relative energy at rest (ball-at-head-height example), excluding kinetic energy in motion. RE sources are kinetic, inexhaustible, and 'incapable of ownership by anyone' -- 'All mankind owns them, and their EDU cannot be limited to the nationals of any state.'

CJ agrees RE should be open to foreigners but his reasoning is geographic, not physics-based: traditional natural resources (petroleum, oil, coal, gold, minerals) in the 'bowels of our land and maritime territory' and the EEZ recognized by Unclos and the 2016 AA 'belong to the Philippines' -- but RE sources like sun, wind, and tides 'are not found solely in the Philippines,' so 'our Charter and its framers could not have intended them for the exclusive EDU of our citizens.'
stances.rhetorical_move: alternative-reasoning differentiation (agree on result, differ on rationale)

stances.claim: Practical and policy considerations reinforce the legal conclusion: RE EDU requires 'tremendous amounts of capital, technological know-how, and risks-taking' PH lacks or has other priorities for; foreign concessionaires cannot viably export the resulting electric power given PH's geographic distance -- 'the logistics of bringing them abroad will just be too complicated and unprofitable' -- so foreigners producing PH RE must sell it to PH; and RE produces 'clean, sustainable, nonpolluting energy that is safe for our planet and healthy for our people.'

Foreign EDU of RE would free PH from foreign oil/coal dependence, preserve foreign exchange reserves, and assure industrial power -- major macro-economic benefits beyond the immediate energy supply. The 'final word' is that all EDU -- whether RE or not, whether potential or kinetic, whether open to foreigners or not -- remains subject to 'the full control and supervision of the State.'

notable_anecdotes: The Article XII Section 2 verbatim quote opening the column -- making the full constitutional text available before introducing the Remulla interpretation that reads it down.
The Latin doctrinal principles named in pair -- noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis -- preserved verbatim as the statutory-construction architecture for Remulla's opinion.

Remulla's ball-drop physics example -- 'if a ball is held up at head height, it has potential energy relative to [the] floor due to gravity. But when the ball is released, its potential energy decreases and such is transformed into increasing kinetic energy until it hits the floor and stops' -- making the abstract energy-state distinction tangible.
The 'All mankind owns them' framing -- converting RE sources into global commons by Remulla's logic, with implications for foreign-investor argumentation across other extractive sectors.

CJ's quiet declaration of alternative reasoning -- 'WHILE I AGREE THAT RENEWABLE ENERGY SHOULD BE OPEN TO FOREIGNERS, not just to Filipinos, my reason is simple' -- modeling the agree-on-result-but-differ-on-rationale move that distinguishes a careful columnist from a relay reporter.

The geographic-uniqueness analytical move -- 'they are not found solely in the Philippines' as the framers'-intent inferential basis -- a textually-modest reasoning that doesn't require contestable physics distinctions.
The 'bowels of our land and maritime territory' phrasing for traditional resources -- evocative anatomical-geographical compression.

The export-impracticability argument -- 'foreigners who undertake the EDU... will not be able to sell them viably except to us... the logistics of bringing them abroad will just be too complicated and unprofitable' -- making the foreign-extraction concern empirically self-limiting.
The final-word state-supervision reservation -- ensuring the column doesn't read as foreign-investor advocacy but as bounded regulatory recategorization.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin 'Boying' Remulla's Department of Justice Opinion No. 21, Series of 2022, which holds that renewable energy (RE) -- 'especially solar, wind, hydro and ocean or tidal energy sources' -- is open to foreign exploration, development, and utilization (EDU). Under Article XII Section 2 of the Constitution, all 'natural resources' and 'all forces of potential energy' are owned by the State, with EDU 'under the full control and supervision of the State' and limited to Filipino citizens or 60%-Filipino-owned entities -- meaning aliens are banned from EDU of such resources and forces. Remulla argues that under the statutory-construction principles noscitur a sociis (interpretation by association) and ejusdem generis (interpretation by class), 'natural resources' covers only resources sharing the characteristic of being 'susceptible to appropriation,' like the enumerated lands, fisheries, forests, and wildlife -- so 'the sun, the wind or the ocean' fall outside because 'they are not subject to appropriation.' Remulla further distinguishes potential energy ('energy at rest,' position-relative -- illustrated by a ball held at head height that loses potential energy and gains kinetic energy as it falls to the floor) from kinetic energy ('energy in motion'), classifying RE sources as kinetic and therefore inexhaustible and 'incapable of ownership by anyone' -- 'All mankind owns them, and their EDU cannot be limited to the nationals of any state.' CJ agrees RE should be open to foreigners but his reasoning is geographic, not physics-based: traditional natural resources like 'petroleum, oil, coal, gold, and other minerals found in the bowels of our land and maritime territory, as well as in our exclusive economic zone' recognized by Unclos and the 2016 Arbitral Award 'belong to the Philippines' and should be reserved solely for Filipinos. But RE sources like sun, wind, and tides 'are not found solely in the Philippines,' so 'our Charter and its framers could not have intended them for the exclusive EDU of our citizens.' Practically, RE EDU 'requires tremendous amounts of capital, technological know-how, and risks-taking that we do not have or are unwilling to undertake'; foreign concessionaires cannot viably export the resulting electric power given PH's distance from other countries -- 'the logistics of bringing them abroad will just be too complicated and unprofitable'; and RE provides 'clean, sustainable, nonpolluting energy that is safe for our planet and healthy for our people,' freeing PH from foreign oil/coal dependence and preserving foreign exchange reserves while assuring 'enough power and energy to turn the wheels of our industries and factories.' The final word: EDU of natural resources, whether renewable or not, whether potential or kinetic, whether open to foreigners or not, remains 'subject to the full control and supervision of the State.'
